title: US Army First Aid Manual FM 4-25.11

provenance.notes: Official public domain military medical and first responder manual.

structure.title: Chapter 1: Emergency Assessment & Immediate Life Measures

sections.title: The ABCs of Emergency Care
sections.text:
In any trauma casualty, prioritize immediate life threats in order:
1. Airway: Ensure the casualty has an open, clear airway without obstruction.
2. Breathing: Assess chest rise, respiratory rate, and bilateral breath sounds.
3. Circulation: Check for catastrophic arterial hemorrhage and carotid/radial pulse.
4. Disability: Evaluate level of consciousness (AVPU: Alert, Voice, Pain, Unresponsive).
5. Exposure: Protect from hypothermia while inspecting all anatomical regions.

sections.title: Airway Obstruction & Head-Tilt Chin-Lift
sections.text:
If the casualty is unconscious and not breathing normally:
1. Perform head-tilt chin-lift maneuver (or jaw thrust if cervical spine injury is suspected).
2. Clear foreign material from the oral cavity with a finger sweep only if visible.
3. Place the casualty in the recovery position (lateral recumbent) if breathing resumes to prevent aspiration of vomit.

sections.title: Tourniquet Application and Direct Pressure
sections.text:
For severe extremity hemorrhage:
1. Apply direct firm pressure with sterile gauze directly over the wound.
2. If bleeding is pulsatile or arterial, apply a windlass tourniquet 5 to 7 cm proximal to the wound (never over a joint).
3. Tighten until bleeding stops and distal pulse vanishes.
4. Mark the casualty's forehead with 'T' and the exact 24-hour time of application.

sections.title: Recognizing and Treating Shock
sections.text:
Hemorrhagic shock is a life-threatening collapse of tissue perfusion.
Signs: Pale, cold, clammy skin; rapid, weak pulse (>100 bpm); tachypnea; thirst; altered mental status.
Treatment:
1. Control all active bleeding immediately.
2. Elevate lower extremities 20 to 30 cm if no spinal or pelvic fractures exist.
3. Keep the casualty insulated from ground cold with blankets.
4. Reassure the patient and do not give fluids by mouth if surgery or airway compromise is possible.

sections.title: Principles of Immobilization
sections.text:
To splint a fractured extremity:
1. Check distal pulse, motor function, and sensation (PMS) before and after splinting.
2. Immobilize the joint above and the joint below the fracture site.
3. Pad rigid splints (sticks, rolled magazines, SAM splints) with cloth to prevent pressure necrosis.
4. Secure firmly with bandages without constricting distal circulation.

structure.title: Chapter 4: Environmental Injuries: Heat & Cold Trauma

sections.title: Heat Exhaustion vs Heat Stroke
sections.text:
Heat exhaustion: Profuse sweating, pale clammy skin, nausea, normal core temperature. Move to shade, loosen clothing, give cool oral electrolyte fluids.
Heat stroke: Medical emergency! Core temperature >40°C (104°F), hot dry or flushed skin, confusion, seizures, loss of consciousness.
Treatment: Rapid aggressive evaporative cooling (strip clothing, spray cool water, fan vigorously, place ice packs in axillae and groin).

sections.title: Hypothermia and Frostbite
sections.text:
Hypothermia occurs when body core temperature drops below 35°C (95°F).
Signs: Shivering, slurred speech, clumsy hands, apathy ('umbles').
Treatment: Remove wet clothing immediately, insulate with dry sleeping bags, provide warm sweet liquids if alert, apply gentle external heat to torso (never rub limbs).
For frostbite: Rewarm frozen tissue in warm water (38-40°C) only if there is zero danger of refreezing.
